editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Good morning. Today's date is November 10, 2012. My name is Robert McAughan. I'm conducting an oral history interview at the Sunbelt Litigation and Reporting Services in Houston, Texas. The court reporter today is B J Orsack. Our veteran this morning is John J. Douglass. His date of birth is March 9, 1922. And he served in the United States Army from April 18, 1943 to January 31, 1974. Mr. Douglass, I guess before we began, you had indicated there was an overview I think that you wanted to provide or some information that you wanted to provide.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Yes; I think it's important to remember that all of us served in World War II. I mean it was a universal sort of thing. I was in college when the war started. And I was in the University of Nebraska where you had compulsory ROTC for the first two years. Everybody -- every male took ROTC the first two years. Well, I was in about the -- about the time the war came along, it had been pretty obvious there was one that I was going to be in it because I was healthy and able to go and intended to go and so on. But, so I went on into advanced ROTC and the idea of advanced ROTC, of course, at that time you would be commissioned as a Second Lieutenant on completing your university. I was one of those lucky ones. That was the only year that they did not immediately commission us because we didn't go to summer camp in the summer between our junior and senior years. So I was in advanced ROTC; and along and about January -- February as a matter of fact of 1943 -- we weren't even signed up for the draft. It wasn't necessary for ROTC students to sign up for the draft. All at once we got called in and they said: You'd better get over to the headquarters. When I came down to the school in the morning and saw all my friends at fraternity house and they said: You'd better get over to ROTC. They're calling all of you together. So I went over there. And they said: We want you to all sign up for the draft. It doesn't mean anything, but it just looks better. We said: Oh, that's fine; and, of course, a week later we got a letter saying you're 1-A. 1-A in those days meant you were going to be drafted. So we -- they said: Don't pay any attention to that. Well, three weeks later, it was in the middle of January -- middle of February, it was the coldest day I've ever seen in Nebraska. And that's saying a lot. And they called us all down on a Saturday morning. And we got in the back of army trucks and road about, early in the morning, from Lincoln to Omaha. And we went to Fort Crook, which is now SAC headquarters. And there they signed us all, they swore us all in to the United States Army. Because they said they wanted us in and a record of us. And we all took a physical exam. And one of the interesting things was that some of us never got our temperature up until way in the afternoon because they were walking us around without any clothes on, as you know, in one of these mass physical exams. And we had our socks on and that was all and pair of pants, of course, underpants. But we had been so cold in that car. So then they said: But we're not calling you in active duty or anything like that. This is just to get all the records. Well, of course, two months later in the middle of April, they called us one day and said: Get over there again to the headquarters so we all went over there. And they said: Here's your new uniforms, put them on. You're now Privates in the Army. So we lived in an unused library that had been built but never used as a library. And for the last six weeks of our -- of my college career, I was a soldier in the Army. And my duty was just to go finish school and then we were graduated. And then there's a couple of funny stories about the fact that they put us on leave for two weeks and then they didn't know what to do with us so they put us on leave for two more weeks. Well, this will be over pretty soon and then they sent us another letter, you're going to be on leave another two weeks. And they said: No; no. They took all of us down to Fort Riley, Kansas. And at Fort Riley, Kansas we went into kind of a basic training thing and they didn't -- the people who were teaching us were old ROTC people and they hadn't been on active duty for many years so they issued us all M1 rifles right out of the cosmoline. Cosmoline is a kind of a grease that you put guns in as you know and weapons. And we took our weapons and we didn't know how to take them apart or disassemble them and there's nobody else there that did either so for five weeks we layout in the hot sun of Fort Riley, Kansas and dry fired. We aimed at targets and pulled the trigger and we did this and then finally somebody came along and said: Enough of this. We all went to ROTC. So they sent all of these ROTC groups from all over the country and sent them to OCS at the same time. Well, they increased -- we got another bargain there because they increased -- if you heard the 90 day wonders. Well, those are the three month people that went to OCS. Well, we got a bargain because we got to go for four months instead of three months.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Any rate, I was commissioned Second Lieutenant of infantry. As a matter of fact on Pearl Harbor Day -- do you know what Pearl Harbor Day is?

sp.speaker: Phillip
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Pearl Harbor Day of 1943 and immediately was called to active duty and I was assigned immediately to the infantry school as an instructor. Now I didn't really know much more than any Second Lieutenant knew; but they were people who were older and smarter and more experienced than I and so they taught me how to -- I taught the anti tank weapons and for a year I remained at Fort Riley, excuse me, at Fort Benning, Georgia as a -- as a Second Lieutenant and promoted to First Lieutenant in the middle of that period, which I was very pleased.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Let me ask you one question if I can because I would be interested -- going back to when you first started at the University of Nebraska, did you have in mind that you were going to have a military career; or was that something that was on your radar?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I was going to be a lawyer. I had been told since I was 12 years old that I was to be a lawyer. Now I didn't have anybody in the family who was a lawyer. There was no reason to believe I should be a lawyer but everybody told me you're -- with a name like that and probably meant that I talked so much. You're going to be a lawyer.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And so I always thought I would go to Nebraska. And I went to Lincoln High School, which is where the university is. And in those days everybody at Lincoln High, if you were able, went on to the University of Nebraska. That's what you did. That's the formal years and so I did and I planned on going to law school after I finished my four years. Well, the war came along and everything changed. Our whole world changed. I think it's important to know that my wife is an Army brat. And she went to war, too. She became -- and went to the office of censorship and she was in the office of censorship and nobody even knows what the office of censorship is. But she read mail in San Antonio for a year or two and then went to Panama where she did secret inks work. And she will never tell me to this day what she did but you knew that's what she was doing was reading mail that was passing from South America, stopped in Panama, opened and then sent on to the United States.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: How did you feel in college when you went in kind of expecting that you were going to go through college, go to law school and probably have a life very different than the one you ended up having and then realizing that the war and the conflict was really going to change your world and change the life that you thought you were going to have?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Oh, we didn't even concern ourself with that. We knew what we were going to do. The world was at war. The world was at war. And we were in it. And I was a healthy strong young 18, 19, 20 year-old man, young man and I knew that I was going to war and the question is well, how would I get there and when would I get there. It wasn't if I would get there or change my life. Everybody was involved. My mother who was a very quiet woman went to work in a bomb factory at Wahoo, 30 miles away.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: At what point did you realize that it was a world war and you're going to be involved? Was that before you were in college? Was that while you were in college?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I came home one night about -- night. Came in. My mother was sitting in the kitchen. I parked my car. I was a very pampered child and I got a car. And neither my mother or father ever drove, but I had a car. I came in about midnight, and we listened to the fact that the Germans had attacked Poland. And I said to my mother: We're going to be at war. She remembers this and I remember it. And we just knew that this was the beginning of a change in our whole life. And as I say after that then everything changed. We got into the war and we got into rationing. And we got into everybody doing and when -- and ROTC was just the next step for me.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It wasn't any question that I was going to do it. I mean, it wasn't any thought that I'm going to change my life-style. I'm going to go out and win the war and then I'll come back and go to law school.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now you had a tremendous military career and obviously are very, very intelligent and educated. Was that experience that you had, you know, recognizing with the Polish invasion that the world had changed and that you're going to be at war, was that something that was experienced by your friends and, you know, like your fraternity brothers in Nebraska or was that something that --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We all knew it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- wasn't appreciated?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: My closest friends in life were my friends in college. But they had been my friends in high school. Because of this as I say Nebraska, Lincoln, you went to Nebraska and then you -- my closest friends were all in ROTC except one fellow, my -- one of my close buddies. And he was drafted, went into CIA. So I mean he was the smart one of the whole bunch. He was really the brilliant young man of our group and he decided not to take ROTC. Anyway, and if you didn't make that decision at a certain point to go on and take advance, you couldn't later come back and say, oh, I wish I stayed.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Now he was later commissioned so it didn't, I mean, he was later -- well, anyway. That answer that question?

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: It did. And I'm curious from kind of looking back historically, you know, now when there's an announcement of conflict or war, people immediately try to take sides or whether it's good or bad and did you see any of that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We had no question that it was a good war. Nobody ever said -- if anybody had said that they were on the side of the Germans, there would have been a finger pointing. I'm from a community of -- had a great group of our -- our minority were called Russians. They weren't really. They come from -- they were Germans who had gone to the Ukraine and then gone back from the Ukraine and then come to the United States. And consequently these were our -- this was our minority in my hometown. And they were not -- they were not in any way opposed to what we were doing. Nobody wanted to go to war. Don't misunderstand me.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We're all smart enough and intelligent enough to know that war isn't fun and it isn't a great thing to do. And war is hell as Sherman said: But it was a war that we felt we had to fight. And everybody was in it. Everybody, as I say. Tell you about my mother and father. My father went to work at the local Air Force base. My mother went, as I said, to -- she was the most unlikely woman to help load a bomb.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It's a wonder they didn't say, well, no; no, don't do it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And I may ask some questions that may be a little different because I think historically we have a lot of records from your world history and your book so I may try to get some perspective information if it's okay. Having gone through the World War II, the Korean war and Vietnam, how do you feel communitywise, because obviously in World War II everybody understood we are on the right side; this has to be done; there's no question of the commitment that people have; and then seeing how that attitude may have changed through Korea and Vietnam, did you see any differences in those three situations?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, quite obviously, first of all, you got to remember by the time you're now questioning me about Korea and Vietnam, I had become a regular Army officer. And so my outlook may have been somewhat different. I was married to a woman who was an Army girl, whose father and mother and whose grandfathers were both Army. So within our family and the people I was dealing with and the friends I had and the people I socialized with were all military so -- but I was, I was a big boy and I recognized that some people didn't like the Korean war. There was a lot of antipathy to the Korean war. First of all, we still had the draft. We still had the draft in the first part of the Vietnam war. As I say, in that first six months, first war, World War I -- II, excuse me -- some of my friends think I'm old enough for World War I. I'm not. But World War II, I was an infantry officer. Now, frankly, I didn't go to combat. I never heard a shot fired in anger. After I spent a year teaching, I was called to -- I got orders -- I got orders on one year to the day. They said: When you teach a year at infantry school, then you'll move. So I thought, this is in the middle of the Battle of the Bulge. And I thought, I know where I'm going.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I'm an Infantry First Lieutenant. And I went to Fort -- came home for Christmas for a leave and my family was all, you know, shaky. What are you going to do? And you're going to go blah, blah, blah and so then I went to Fort Meade and waited for my orders. And I waited for my orders. And I waited for my orders. And then once I saw that I was connected with a whole bunch of Lieutenant Colonels and Majors and Captains, and I was only a Lieutenant --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- in this shipment. Well, what in the world is this? What am I doing? And I was sent to Panama. I don't know why I got sent to Panama. I had no connections. I had no political connections, had no connections of any kind, I had no military connections. Somehow, somebody picked up a number and said: We need one more Lieutenant, First Lieutenant in Panama.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: So I went to Panama. And I became an executive officer of an infantry company, which eventually was on what is called lock guard duty. And we went out and I took my troops and we had them at -- at Meraflores at the Locks on the Atlantic side; and then later when the war was coming to an end, things began to get different. And I was moved, and I became a public relations officer. And I became very fortunate because it got rid of everybody who wanted to get off. Now the one thing you find out about the end of World War II, as soon as it ended, everybody wanted out. Well, I didn't have enough numbers and everything was how many months you spend.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And how many months you spend at a particular place before you can get out. Well, I didn't have a enough numbers so I was going to be kept for another year at least and I became public relations officer for the whole command. That was a pretty big deal if you might imagine. I was a Captain. I was a Lieutenant as a matter of fact when I got there. And the Three-Star General called me in one day and said: This is an interesting aspect of the world. Called me in one day and said he was going to promote me to Captain and he did. And he said to me: How long were you a Second Lieutenant? And I said: Six months. How long were you a First Lieutenant? And I said: Eighteen months. And he said: Not very long, was it? Well, it seemed like it was forever to me.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Why wasn't I promoted earlier? He said: Do you know how long I was a Second Lieutenant? Three years. You know how long I was a Captain? Seven years. You know how long I was full Colonel? One month. You know how long I was a Brigadier General? Two months. He said: Young man, it's all relative. And I have made that one of my keys in my whole life since then. All these things are relative what the time and the place is and that's how I got to Panama. As my wife and I say, we'd never have met if I hadn't gone down there. We wouldn't have three children. We wouldn't have had eight grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: You met her in Panama?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Met her in Panama. She was one of the few American women there. And we managed to find where they were. Of course, there were a lot of American women.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Canal zone employees and they were all our friends. But I kind of gravitated to her and she to me. We were both college graduates and so forth.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: How did the group in Panama feel, for example, you thought you were going to be shipped off to the Battle of the Bulge and immediately being in the midst of a very aggressive, intense combat and found that you were shipped to Panama. How -- how did you feel and how did people feel in that role? Were they relieved? Were they upset? Did they -- did they -- what was the attitude in general of the groups that were not shipped because you can see in one sense there would be a great sense of relief and then on the other sense there may be some different emotions?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: You're not going.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: You're not doing it. And, of course, in my whole life there has been a feeling that I wasn't there. And there's nothing I can do about it. Nothing I could have done about it then. You didn't -- you didn't -- First Lieutenants didn't say I want it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Here, this is where I ought to go.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I was certain I was on two different orders and we never know what happened. I was on one draft order as they kind of call it early and then I was taken off of that one and put on a second one. I don't know why. Somebody was saying to me, you know, you're not going to go.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Like you say, it's all relative. You look at what that meeting your wife and everything that happened there. They are all --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I had buddies that went --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- out of ROTC, people very close to me in every way. Well, to go on, as I say, I got -- I started to get out of the Army then. I said: Well, it's time to get out now. I've all my numbers. And I came home and in the meantime I'd had gotten very interested in this lady. And she came -- we happened to go back to the United States on the same ship. And things developed even greater, as you might imagine. And I said: Well, why don't you come up and visit my parents. I thought she ought to know me better than just me.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And -- because we were not of the same backgrounds at all. Same college, same everything else; but -- so she came up, and she was there. I asked her to marry me. And then at that point I become kind of disabused. I had been home about two or three weeks, from walking around and I tried to get -- I tried to see what I was going to do. I immediately went down and entered law school. That was all it took. Didn't have to go through a lot of SAT's, that sort of things.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I went up to law school. Said: Okay, fine. Class will begin next whatever it was. And so then I said: No, I think I'll go back in the Army for two years. I don't like this attitude. I don't like the attitude of America right now.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, what was the attitude you saw?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Attitude was there were a lot of guys living on 52-20, what was called 52-20. You could sit around for 52 weeks and draw some money even though you're -- just didn't have a job. And everybody was kind of, I didn't like the attitude. I thought this will calm down. America will change in two years.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And the 52-20 program, was that a veterans program?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: So the veterans come back and would get some amount of money for 52 weeks?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Yeah. If you weren't working --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- and they weren't working. And I went to the Veterans Club and watched there and I said: This isn't for me. I'm not -- I don't want to get into this. I want to go back to work.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: So I asked my wife to marry her -- marry me and she said she would. And then we agreed, why didn't I just go back in the Army for a couple of years and we'll get this straightened out. In the meantime I'll go -- come back and I can always come back and go to law school. I knew that.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: So I went back in the Army and I happened to know through my own little nosiness that my job had never been filled in Panama. Nobody had ever taken that job as Public Relations Officer for the Command. So I did something, the most gutty thing I've ever done, never done anything like it again. I called the Pentagon and said: I would like to go back to Panama. My wife is there. I know the job hasn't been filled and so forth. Believe it or not, I was sent back to Panama. Well, I now know later that General Crittenberger knew about this. And he arranged it --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- as a matter of fact.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: He had heard --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I had thought it was my phone call. It had nothing to do with my call.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Oh, you were sent there totally independent of the call?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, he knew about it --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- and made an arrangement. When I got back I went to work for him for another three years. Except that he left and was replaced by General Matthew Ridgway, who is one of the great American soldiers as you know and worked for him for the rest -- for two years.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now what day-to-day -- what kind of the challenges you faced as the PR officer in Panama?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Oh, all sorts of things. I remember there was a plane came back from the United States carrying the sons -- sons of officers and people in Panama, the cadets from West Point, who were on leave for their summer leave. When they came in, the plane hit the mountain. And I immediately got a call to go there. When I got, there General Crittenberger was there with me; and the Chief of Staff said: I've already put out a press release. And the -- General Crittenberger said to him: You don't put out press releases. He puts out press releases.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And so that's the kind of things -- we had lot of relationships. Quite obviously the Commanding General in Panama was the Commanding General of all sources, when I talk about Ridgway and Crittenberger. And so there was a lot of relationships with all people in South America politically, militarily, diplomatically. And we had lots of visits. And my responsibility was to watch these things, and I got calls all the time from the press. There were two English language newspapers in Panama. And there was an Associated Press rep and there was a New York Times press representative and there was a Time magazine representative, all stationed in Panama. And so I was the outlook for all the news that came out. I mean I was --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- I was just a voice. I wasn't making any policy or anything.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. Right. Now in corporate PR departments the goals often is to create a good image of the company and then get particular messages across. With the military at that time, were you primarily viewing your role that way or were there particular messages or signals or --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Of course, we were --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- or information you wanted to send?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- trying to get along with Panamanians. Let's face it, there's a very tight relationship with Panama at that time. It was -- they had put up with us during the war and all but we were in the town and we did have a lot of clout so we were watching their newspapers very closely. And both of those English language newspapers of which I speak had half the paper came out in English and half the paper came out in Spanish. And when you got the morning paper, you got the Spanish and English together. But we had to be very -- we were trying to maintain a position. And, of course, the Governor of the Panama Canal was a military Major General. So we had a Lieutenant General so the -- in the pecking order, the problems came to him, not to me. But it was the kind of thing that I was concerned with, and they were very anxious to have the Army there, have the troops there and so forth. Because I can tell you some things about when I was at Fort Riley how strongly they were pushing the Army. But at any rate that was -- as I say, then I learned about -- heard about a program. The Army had to send people to advanced training and I heard about getting a masters degree in public relations or whatever it's called now. It isn't called that anymore. And so I began to dicker about that. And I had a good friend who was the Judge Advocate of the Panama Canal Department, Military Department and because I had known his son, his brother, excuse me. His brother had been a member of the Senior Men's Honorary the year following me so I knew him very well. And I got to know the Judge Advocate. And he said: Why don't you go to law school? I said: Well, that's what I always planned to do. He said: We've got a program to send you to law school. Why don't you take this test? And I did and strangely enough I passed and I was selected. And they said: Where do you want to go? They said: You can have three choices. And I chose -- I thought: Well, I think I'd like to go to Michigan. So I put down Michigan first choice. And when I -- so in 1949 when I finished my tour in Panama, I was sent to the University of Michigan Law School. By that time we had one baby.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And we went to Ann Arbor. We left Panama after my wife had been there almost five years. And I had been there almost four years in the tropics. And the first morning we arrived in Ann Arbor, it was 40 degrees. And she was ready to turn around and go back.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Be that as it may, I went through law school.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And were you active military during that time?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: All the time I was active military. I was an officer in the Army. I -- in the summer, I was directed to get a job as an intern some place. To find a place where I could be an intern and learn so they -- I got a internship with a very fine firm in Ann Arbor with a man, the man who kind of took care of me in that firm and was a Annapolis graduate, later became a Federal District Judge, so I learned a lot.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And who was that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I wish you hadn't asked.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It's on the tip of my tongue but I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: At any rate, I don't remember his name at this point; but it's in there some place.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Okay. Great.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: At any rate, when we finished law school, I was admitted to practice. Took the bar exam in Nebraska and in Michigan and passed, so I had to pass the bar exam in order to be able to practice law in the Army. And so when I got my orders, I was ordered to the Pentagon. Well, I was ordered to the Pentagon because, I'm pretty sure, this friend of mine who had started me going to law school, Reggie Miller, had wanted, he was going to be my kind of rabbi you might call it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure. And what year was that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: This was 1952.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: So I went to the Pentagon. And I was on the list. At that time all promotions were on a national list. They were not made locally. And a friend of mine who was in law school, both us were on that list. And I was on the list for Major and so I was waiting yet to be a Major in the Army, where you have that stuff on my hat and all that stuff. And I got to Washington; and they put me to work, in teaching me. And I was writing opinions and so forth in the Pentagon. And after I had been there about two months, unfortunately, my quote, rabbi, committed suicide and strangely enough a month later I got orders to Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now I know that's probably maybe a difficult issue to talk about. Do you know what may have led to that? Was it a personal issue or something related to war experience?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Personal issue. Personal issue. I think I've lost my -- my pusher and so they said: Send him over to Korea and see what he can do.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now at that time and this will show some of my lack of history, when you went to the Pentagon in 1952, what was your prospective on the likelihood of major war or conflict, I mean --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, we were in the war. Korea had started.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Korea had started in 1950. And we had been there, and we were at the point now where they were going through this exercise of are we going to get peace in Korea or not? And there was still a lot of fighting going on, much of it. And as a matter of fact, I had written to General Ridgway -- when General Ridgway went to -- to take command in Korea, I had written a note to him that although I was going to law school, that if he thought that I could be of any help, telling him I supported him strongly, that I was there.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: He didn't indicate although we've had a lot of correspondence through the years. At any rate, so I went to Korea, went to Japan and stopped there and said: Hello. And then I went to Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now when you went to World War II, you clearly in that one personally felt that was something that absolutely had to be done, the world is at war, and the right needs to take care. What were your thoughts and emotions going into Korea?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: My job was, when I went to Korea was, that I was in the Army and I was to go where I was sent.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: So was it more of a job responsibility?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, I didn't even think about it any other way. I didn't have to like the war in Korea. But I thought we were right, certainly. I thought that when North Koreans for no reason attack South Korea, I realized it was a disaster. And then, of course, when the Chinese came in on it and I had friends, of course, who had gone in -- who had not gone into JAG but in infantry or otherwise and I knew they had gone to Korea, I had no misgivings if you are -- of any kind about going. I thought I ought to go.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It would have been nice, I suppose, to stop off in Japan instead of going to Korea. And rather amusing when I got to Korea, they said: We're going to send you down to be the adviser to the Republic of Korea Judge Advocate General. And that's where this thing comes from, the picture there.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure. And I want to talk about that in a minute. Let me ask kind of a perspective question.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And I know you're at a different point in your life as a man. And so you would have different attitudes but I'd like to know if you felt and the people around you felt differently about the enemy in World War II and how you would feel about the enemy in Korea, whether it was the same kind of emotion, the same kind of thought; or they were both viewed as the other side with the same degree of intensity?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't think I thought in either case of them as individuals. I thought of them as we are -- we are involved with a group or enemy who have -- who are trying to take position that is not within our best interest in both cases. I didn't have any question about that. And consequently there was no question in my mind that -- I mean, as I look back on it. Now this is a long time ago. You got to remember this is 60 years ago.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And you're asking me to tell you today what I thought 60 years ago. I didn't have any misgivings. Now I left my wife and two children by this time. And they drove -- they went down to San Antonio where they lived with her mother and father, and we communicated by mail. I was a young man. She was a young woman. We were a friendly family. Everything was good about the family. And I was -- didn't have any -- I didn't want to go and leave them particularly.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It's not saying, oh, isn't this nice? I'm going to get away for two years so I went to Taegu to be the adviser to the ROK Advocate General.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And let me, I just got another question on this. From historical perspective when we look back at World War II and now we know about all the atrocities that the Germans and Nazis engaged in, I think it's very easy to classify them as one of the great evils of the world, that no rational, moral person would ever think that that was appropriate, and then we look at Korea which may have been more of a political situation with the Soviet Union involved, did any of that come through at that time; or was it simply they're the enemy, they're opposite us; and we feel this way; or was there a, you know, a difference in some kind of a moral outrage?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't think I really knew. I don't think that I really knew about the Holocaust. I mean, yeah; but I really didn't know about it until the war was over.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I mean, at the time I entered the Army, this was not a matter. When I was getting ready to go to -- when I thought I was going to Battle of the Bulge and didn't go, I thought that -- I didn't know about Malmedy. I knew that they were fighting in the cold and it was harsh.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And it was difficult and so forth. But I look at it as two armies. I think I felt that this was an international problem in 1952 and '3 when I went to Korea. It was 1953 when I get there, in February of '53, by the time you go through all the business.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But I didn't feel that I was -- I didn't ever feel that it was an individual, me against some other --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- person. I thought it was me in the United States; and I was the representative in the United States through the United States Army to be doing this. Now I had changed my -- from being an infantry officer to being a JAG officer.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I was frankly kind of disappointed that they sent me to advise the Judge Advocate General of the Korean army. I wanted to be up in one of the units where I thought something was going on. But you go where you go.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And it was a good experience for me. Because I have often joked, it was probably really foolish for me to be trying to advise the ROK Advocate General because I didn't know beans. I'd only been a lawyer for six months.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Let me ask you: We can take just maybe a short break. I know you have a picture there that I may want to talk about if we can.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And before I talk about the picture, again from my generation looking back at Korea, a lot of it seemed to have been driven by the U.S./Soviet conflict?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: China/U.S./Soviet.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And was that something that was appreciated by you and those around you --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- in the '50s?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Of course. Of course. I mean intellectually at least we knew about it. I mean I didn't see any Russians, but more important we were concerned about the Chinese.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Don't forget that we were within, within a very close situation to MacArthur leading us into China. I might say I was like -- well, I was not a great believer in MacArthur. And I thought this was one of the worse things that we could have done. I knew that much about world affairs.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: I've got a couple of follow-up questions on that. In today's world where you have 24-hour news channels and the internet and blogs, there's so much political information and geopolitical information out there, how was it that it became understood? Was it that the Chinese-Russian conflict in Korea, was that something that was distributed throughout the military or was that something that the public appreciated?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Everybody knew it in the United States and that's why there was a conflict. The people didn't want to get in -- much of the conflict in my mind -- now remember I'm talking 60 years ago. Much of the conflict was not that we didn't want to win the war. But that we didn't want to get into a greater war. It's a fear. It's a fear of a greater war.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It's my fear today of a greater war.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I'm not worried about Afghanistan. I mean they've driven every other people out of there. They can drive us out.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. So is trying to go between two curves trying to win the war in Korea but not be so aggressive or disruptive to create a broader war with China or Russia?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: That's right. And particularly China. I mean, don't forget Chiang Kai-shek just left.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. And I guess in that role, especially since you had some direct dealings with the Koreans who may have had a different situation, did you see any potential escalation into a broader Chinese conflict in your role as a JAG?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I think clearly that Koreans knew they had to rely on us because they needed us for money, equipment, everything else. They couldn't have gone off on their own. It could not have been a frolic of their own. They knew that and they were smart enough and they're smart people. Let's face it. They knew where they were going --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- and what their limitations were. And so I don't think there's ever any question of that. It was what we were going to do. And it's awfully easy to sit in Washington to decide what you're going to do.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: At any rate, it was an interesting year for me, or nine months, that I stayed in there. And as I say my -- I got to know these two or three Korean generals who are lawyers. And --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Let me -- I hate to interrupt but one of the things you said I think would be very interesting to get a record on. You talked about MacArthur and the question of whether it was wise to push into China and you know he's kind of a polarizing figure in a lot of ways. You know, a lot of people think a lot of great things about him. A lot of people think he had certain issues and, you know, very driven in his own direction.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: He was an egotist.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: What were your, I guess, when did you first begin to get exposed to MacArthur and have an impression of him; and how did that change from then until the point in Korea where, you know, you had these concerns?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: 1944, '45 when he was doing these things in the Philippines and Australia and all through the Far East, I mean he was an egomaniac then. That's -- I mean, he was a great leader. And that isn't -- I don't know that he's a great leader. That may be wrong. But he was a great military thinker. But I think he got carried away with his own importance. We all do.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: I guess in the '40s in World War II, I mean did you ever -- was your first reaction to him that, you know, egomaniac, kind of driving for himself; or was that something that developed over time as you saw what he was doing?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I think it developed through the years as we saw it. I mean, when he was attacked in the Philippines, certainly we were -- we were terribly sympathetic to him. There was a little feeling, well, why didn't he get out? But we've understood that. And, you know, all of these things and then the relationships he had with Truman and so on. I mean you begin to think of that down the line pretty soon you know.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And was that something that you felt or do you feel that was a general feeling among the military?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't know how the -- I think that's an unfair question for me if you don't mind. I don't know what others felt. I know how I felt. And I didn't ever discuss is with anybody. I mean it was never discussion for us.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I'm a little outspoken sometimes. And I've been told that. And, anyway, I would just -- it was my view. I once wrote a letter to the what, to the Army Navy Journal, after he left after the -- after the Truman-MacArthur episode. And I said: I thought that, somewhat of a view I'm taking now, that he has to -- he's not the commander-in-chief, something like that. I don't know. I got it in my file some place because nobody really reads what I write anyway.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, as a PR person, I think a lot of people have. I'd be curious from a public relations perspective, someone who has actually been involved in that, one thing about MacArthur, he obviously had a good PR machine, right? I mean, was that something that you thought he had; or did he actually have his own group of people to do that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: He had psychophant.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And how did you come to know that or believe that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, history. What I've read. At this -- the next step of this is that I moved to Japan after Korea; and he had gone by then. But you saw his footsteps, the footprint there in many things that was done. And -- but, you know, what am I? I'm a major. He's a Four-Star General. What do I know? I wasn't -- I had no insight into any information about him --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- I mean at my level. I saw what happened with him and what he did, and I could evaluate in my own mind, but I didn't have any insight particularly.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And we'll go back to Korea in just a minute but on this topic talking about after you went from Korea to Japan after MacArthur had left, what did you see; and what did you feel like he had done there that was either good or bad or needed to be corrected or dealt with?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, my personal reaction today and I think then, that he had made them our friends. I mean what he had done had been an almost unbelievable -- don't forget we dropped the bomb on them.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We had -- not only that, but our planes had fire bombed Tokyo and Yokohama and so on. And I never had anybody spit on me in Japan. I never had anybody other than be nice. Now maybe that -- but something happened -- somebody -- something worked.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. And you see, you know, even today in the Balkans, people have grudges going back to the 1600s; and within a period of a couple of decades, things have changed from Japan being our enemy that we're dropping a fire bomb --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I went back in 1954.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And what do you think -- what do you think played into that? Do you think that was the Japanese culture or do you think that was something unique that MacArthur did or it was some other --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I'm not a good enough analyst to know but something changed and he didn't hurt it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. Was there anything else you saw?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: They looked to a great leader you know.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And he was and he paraded through town and so forth you know and so they looked to him. And let's face it, the constitution he, quote, he wrote for them, unquote. Has been pretty -- it was generally not -- we were not vindictive.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We were not vindictive. I have friends that for many years were pretty bitter about the Japanese. And I suggest you read that book, the new one, what's the name of it? Untroubled, is that it? Or the new one by the woman who wrote Seabiscuit. You ought to read it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Okay. I think I will after this.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It's unbelievable. It's about the American Olympic mile runner who was captured by the Japanese who was shot down.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Oh, yes. I know who you're talking about.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Untroubled, I think. Is that the name of it?

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Yes; yes. I think it is.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It's a fantastic book. Keep it for him.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: I will. We have it at home. His brother has it. Let me go back to Korea. So you had a nine-month span?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Nine-month span there.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And you were assigned to the ROK?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I was assigned to what was called the MAG, Military Advisory Group. Every ROK unit of any kind had an American adviser. Of any kind. The doctors, the lawyers, the division commanders, the logisticians, everybody had an American adviser. And we had -- I wrote a paper after the -- some place about three or four years after I got home, about the military justice system. And I said: We imposed it on them. We took our Uniform Code, wasn't Military Code, 1928 manual and gave it to them and said: Now this is your law.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, this is silly. I mean, it didn't meet their needs at all. I mean, it wasn't -- I mean, you don't just impose something like that. You write it. One of the things we do in the American Army is when somebody does something bad, little piddly stuff, misdemeanor type things in the Army, you fine them so to speak. You withhold their pay. Well, if you're giving somebody 15 cents a month, what good does it do to withhold their pay?

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And that's the kind of thing we gave them to do.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Were you involved in the decision to take our Code and tell them this is their Code?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No, that was before I got there.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: So you arrived and that had been done?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It had been done. Oh, it had been done before the war had started. I mean, we had an advisory group there before the war started in which we were giving them -- telling them how to run the world.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And then your job was basically to now help them implement this Code?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No. Not only help them but help them generally --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- to do things and talk about the law and so forth.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And you've got a picture you brought with you today that's been marked as picture number five. Can you tell us what that is?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Yes. This is a picture taken in the office of the then Judge Advocate General of the ROK Army. And I forgotten how to pronounce his name. Sahn I think it is, the way it's pronounced. And he is giving me a certificate showing my membership in the Republic of Korea Bar Association. This is not a military orientation. This was their civilian bar.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I was number 65. And I have that certificate in glass and always kept it in my office until about a year ago when I finally retired from the University of Houston and sent that to the Judge Advocate General School for some of their momentos. I thought it was interesting and they apparently were glad to receive it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now was there -- you mentioned the way the Military Justice System was basically given to them of being such an early member of the bar, number 65, was their overall legal system something they developed or was that something --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: They were just developing it, yes. They were developing it. And, of course, they had had for many years a Japanese system of law. And when we came in, we began trying to put some more western views into their law. Now I don't know what's happened since. I've become acquainted with a number of Japanese lawyers. As a matter of fact, I brought several here to Houston. I -- my post military career was to run the National College of District Attorneys. I was the Dean of the college here in Houston for 20 years. And I had sort of an international flare so I would try to bring these people here --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- from time to time. And so I got to know some of these people. And they've developed a -- and I'm talking about the civil side particularly. They have -- they've become -- it's very important to them because they're businessmen.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Correct.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And so they have to have the -- the rule of law works. If you don't have the rule of law, business is never going to work as you know.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Okay. Well, I'm getting aside. I'm not talking philosophy so...

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, I think that's important though. When you first went to Korea, it sounds like your role was more extensive than simply helping them implement the Military Code of Justice. It sounded like you were an overall legal adviser to them --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, we tried to talk --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- generally?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- to them about the law, yes. I don't remember subjects particularly, but I remember talking with them. And, of course, sometimes difficult because they were not on our wavelength for some types of the law, but I think they certainly are now.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: What was the biggest difference, if you can remember, between the approach that the western societies took and you saw they were doing?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I can't remember that. I'm sorry. It's been too long ago.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure. I guess, do you remember any kind of interesting experiences you had while you were in Korea, anything either funny or odd or frightening or that you think would be worthy --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I remember my first helicopter flight, first time I had one. We had a, in addition to our job as advising Judge Advocate General, we also had a responsibility for the legal affairs of the MAG, that is the Military Advisory Group, but there were a lot of them. It was a big organization. It was located down in Taegu. It's in the kind of central part of Korea, the big organization. And I remember we had a little -- I don't even remember what the offense was. But we had some offense committed way up by -- in one of the MAG units. And so I flew up there in my first helicopter flight. And I talked to the Lieutenant Colonel, who was the battalion -- who was the Lieutenant Colonel adviser to the ROK Unit that was up there because it was his man that he had brought the charges against. And I thought this fellow looked like a pretty good guy and Lieutenant Colonel Stilwell, who turned out later it was Lieutenant General Stilwell, who I was later to meet in Vietnam. But it was my first flight.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I thought that was pretty great to fly up there and talk about this little problem they had. Anyway that's...

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And what did you think? I mean, that was your first helicopter ride, I assume?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I didn't realize I was going to live in one --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now again maybe kind of a perspective question since you've been through through so much. The type of offenses that you saw occurring in the Korean conflict as compared to the kind of offenses you saw in Vietnam, were they essentially the same; or were they different?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Human beings remain pretty much the same. I mean, you put guns in the hands of people, they have a tendency to use them. You put money in the sight of people, they have a tendency to steal it. You have power in the hands of people and they begin to use it. And I thought that our treatment of Koreans was generally pretty good. I didn't see people beaten and mistreated. But you got to remember, I was not in the forefront of criminal justice.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Because I was -- we didn't have enough American problems at that point. Now they may have up in the divisions but I wasn't a part of them. And I was down here worrying about these problems that I had of my own, because there were only two officers. I had a superior who was, in fact, during my nine months I had three superiors, three different bosses who came in. They didn't last very long. I guess I drive people away. But, anyway, but there were just the two of us in the office; and we had a Korean employee; and I guess that was an enlisted man. And that was all we had in the office. We were pretty much on our own.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh. And in Korea were you distant from the actual conflict?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Yes; we were distant from the conflict.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And in both, kind of another perspective question, in Korea and Vietnam, you had kind of battles going on within countries, so in both instances you had a civilian population that may be supporting the enemy, that would not look that different from those that were helping you?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Not true, not true.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: True in Vietnam. Not true in Korea. There was a battle line in Korea. Now that isn't quite -- I mean I don't mean to be so insistent in that.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But we knew where the battle was. We didn't know where the battle was in Vietnam. Every night I lived in a -- not every night. Most nights in Vietnam I lived in a very large headquarters. And almost certainly, often I'll put it this way, I don't remember how often, often we had incoming at night.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We slept -- first thing when I got there, I lived -- after the some -- one of the -- something happened in Louisiana and there was a whole lot of trailers put out to take care of the people who were affected.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: They sent all those trailers to Vietnam and so they scattered them all over the country, and Colonels lived in those trailers, two to a trailer. And the first thing they gave us was a steel helmet and a flap jacket, and we were supposed to -- as soon as we heard burrb-burrb-burrb-burrb-burrb at night, we were supposed to put on our hat, put on our helmet, put on our flap jacket and run to the bomb shelter. Well, you do this the first six or eight times and then you go enough of that stuff and you don't get hit and so I put my flap vest alongside my bed; and then I sleep through it. I never told my wife this, I mean at the time.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But you get kind of used to that. It's like we always carried a weapon when we -- I had a driver and a car, when I was in Vietnam because I was a senior lawyer in Vietnam, senior army lawyer. And I was driving back and forth. I had an office in Saigon, big office. Had all the claims office. There was 50 people there paying claims and then I had the office out there about 50 miles away at Long Binh. And we drive back and forth. When I first got there, we always made sure that we were carrying weapons. And I remember toward the end of my tour, I said to my driver one time: You got your weapon? No. Did you bring yours, sir? No. I mean we got very complacent about it. And it wasn't that there was any less reason to do it. We just became complacent.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And was that because you felt like --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I hadn't been hit yet.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- whatever was going to happen was going to happen?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't know. We were stupid.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I think -- you just -- I don't know what I, you know, what are you going to do with a weapon if you're driving along the road and you're bombed.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure. You went through the three: World War II, Korea and Vietnam. I would be curious about kind of like your personal perception of danger and stress. And I know you were in different locations in all of those. How was it that different between the three because obviously in Vietnam --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Only place I had any stress was in Vietnam. And that was -- I mean we never knew where you were going to be safe in Vietnam. I mean, the enemy was there, but there wasn't any line. The only line was the stupidity that we fought the war with in which we said: We won't go over the dividing line between North and South Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, that's -- as far as I'm concerned that's just dumb.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: That's the stupidity of the war, the Korean war or --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Vietnam war. We went -- the stupidity of the Korean war was we went over the line without knowing what was coming.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now I wanted to maybe wrap up the Korean discussion a little bit and then move on to Vietnam. In Korea over the nine months there, what do you think was the most significant incident you would have been involved with the ROK JAG?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't think that there was anything really outstanding to the truth matter. There's a lot of the things going on. We were still doing this thing about trying to get peace up there. And you remember there was a -- we had captured a lot of North Koreans and put them on an island. Well, there was going to be something called Big Switch. And we were going to switch, Big Switch or Little Switch, I forgotten the name. We were going to release all of those people and then they were going to release a lot of our prisoners. We were going to make a Big Switch. Well, when we got ready to switch theirs, they didn't want to go.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: They didn't want to go back?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No. And so that happened during the period that I was -- I remember this very well. But I had no relationship with it. I'm just saying we were doing something else. Now I was --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: What happened in that incident? Did they compel them to go back?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No. They didn't. Of course, we wouldn't do that.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And did that impact our ability to get our prisoners?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It impacted the peace negotiations. That was the problem. We wanted our people back and our people would have been happy to come.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But then when the whole thing was over, there was a Big Switch. And we did the switch. But I think the first one was called a Little Switch as I recall. It's been too many years.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And were you involved in that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I wasn't involved in that. At the time the war ended, quote, I had been out of Korea for some time.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Now in Korea as opposed to Vietnam, you talk about the war ending but even today there's the parallel drawn. You've got soldiers on both sides.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: The war is not over.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And from your personal belief as someone who has experienced that, do you feel a different sense of either closure or nonclosure between Korea where you still have battle lines drawn and weapons facing; and Vietnam where we are having more normalized relationships with them as a country?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Eight years ago I took my son, who is a big grown man. And we went to Vietnam. And we started in North Korea, I mean, North Vietnam; and we had a great time. We traveled all over. We traveled by car. We had people driving us. I mean, we weren't driving ourselves. I wasn't driving up to Omaha or something, but we -- so it was entirely different. Go out today.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I mean, the Vietnamese kids that are here all speak better English than he does probably.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't mean that either.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But they do. I mean within a year they're all speaking perfect English.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. And you look at North Korea where it is today --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: North Korea is -- you would not think of bringing North Koreans here unless they were escaping.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And, of course, they try to escape all the time and they try to go to China and China doesn't want them and I don't think the South Koreans want them very much.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We haven't made any effort. But we're happy to get the Vietnamese. It's a totally different situation and I don't know why. Because it's one country, that's one of the reasons. But that's not my business.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. It's interesting to get your reflection. I mean, do you think in Vietnam the westernized ideals that were brought over by the American soldiers in the south because of the way the war ended have all kind of molded together with the north, whereas in Korea, they've still been very separated?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, of course, the separation makes all the difference. They've not had any opportunity, the North Koreans, to be assimilated at all. And they certainly haven't assimilated the South Koreans.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Okay. I think it would be helpful to maybe explain a little bit of your life from when you left Korea and then how you wound up in Vietnam. Was there an intermediate period?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Of course, yes. I left and went to Japan for two and a half years. We had another baby. I came back, and I went to Fort Sam Houston for a nice tour and then went to the Commanding General Staff College at Fort Leavenworth for a year. And at a time when America was -- the American Army was very, very concerned about nuclear weapons and the impact of nuclear weapons. Then I went from there -- I went to the Pentagon. And I was the head of the Fraud Branch in the Pentagon and people said: That was a particularly smart appointment because it takes one to know one. And that's not true. I said that.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But at any rate, I was there. And then I went to the Army War College. And this was a real -- and I was very pleased to be able to spend a year at Leavenworth and then a year at Carlisle. I was among people who were on the make in each case. These are -- the people that go to Leavenworth are those on the make? People that go to Carlisle, are those on the make? It was great to have the opportunity to hear them and talk to them and be with them. And so I -- from there I went to -- from War College I went to Germany for three years with my family, which was great. We were in Heidelberg for a whole three years. I was the executive officer for the large JA office, U. S. Army in Europe. And it was a great experience for us, and we loved it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Let me ask you some questions about some of the things you talked about. The discussion of the fact that while you were going through these programs, everybody was so concerned about nuclear war. For people like me and my son who have basically grown up with the world where weapons are disseminated more broadly, what -- what kind of impact did that have on you and people's perception of war, if you recall? Was it changing the way people looked at these conflicts or potential conflicts?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I was in War College during Cuba, and my family was in Washington D.C. And I was scared to death because I knew what a nuclear weapon could do. Now I don't -- I mean, the thing we did in Leavenworth when I was there was talk about the impact of a nuclear weapon and what it would do. I mean we understood it very carefully. Remember the -- when the little kids, maybe you, used to go under the -- taught to go under the desk.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And have you seen, when you were in Japan, did you have opportunity to see Hiroshima and Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No, I did not. As a matter of fact, that's one of the great disappointments in my life. I could have. All I had to do was get on the train and go. And I went all over Japan, my wife and I did. We're great travelers. We have been everywhere. I didn't. She tells me that, she reminds me of that about every six months. We never got to see Hiroshima. But I have -- the one thing I learned in Leavenworth, this is a terrible thing. And we were talking then about what was the first stages of nuclear weapons.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And what they could do. And I know that I have no interest, I have no insight into what today is coming along; but I'm very upset about the whole situation in Iran, Iraq, et cetera.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Do -- you mentioned at that same time you were going through programs with people that were on the make or on the move?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: At that time was there -- were there -- what was the perception of the likelihood of any other major conflicts? Did people think it was inevitable?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It was cold war. The cold war. We were scared, I mean, not scared.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We were apprehensive and that apprehension went on certainly at least until Cuba.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, you say at least until Cuba. Did you feel like Cuba had a tension relief?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I think both parties finally realized what they could have done to each other.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Nowadays, you know, very recently there have been stories about how truly close we came to a nuclear conflict in Cuba, I mean, submarines.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Was that something that was understood or appreciated or thought about at the time, or did people really look at the news stories and look at the boats turning back?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't think the people, all people understood it. I know that those of us were in the military understood it, if we had done -- taken some of the training I had. I had a jet friend of mine who was a Major General, still in Washington. And I told my wife, you call him. And if he moves his family, you move.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh. Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I mean, I had no -- I had no insight as to what was going to happen. Don't misunderstand me. I mean, I was just like anybody else reading the paper.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I had no access to classified information. And I don't think anybody else did, frankly. But I knew he was in the Pentagon. He was then a Brigadier General. And I said: If he moves her, you move.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And we're going to move onto Vietnam in a minute. But it sounds like the Cuban missile crisis, from your perspective, was kind of a very significant event. Was it? And if not, what would have been the other thing that maybe changed your perspective on war or conflict over the time you're in the military?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I don't understand your question.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, I guess -- you talked about nuclear weapons and the major destruction it can have, kind of have and a big impact maybe on what a conflict would mean to the world or to the parties involved. Was that -- did that really change your perspective on conflict and war and how it should be fought or the risks or consequences?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Oh, of course. I mean, you can't help it change your conflict, I mean, it's -- it's here. We don't -- there's nothing we can do about it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I mean, I feel very strongly. Well, I don't want to get into what I feel very strongly about today. But I think it's a terrible thought, that the first one is dropped in war. And it's only been two dropped in war. And God willing, there will never be another one dropped. Because I'm afraid the next time there's one dropped, it will be more than one. Somebody is going to retaliate.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I don't want any retaliation because I don't want any first one.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. Absolutely. Now when you were first assigned to Vietnam, what was the year? And what was your initial role at that time?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: All right. I was stationed at Fort Riley and I went back to Washington. And I came on a short trip and I came back. And my wife said to me: You volunteered to go to Vietnam, didn't you? And I said: Yes. And I said: I want the top job in Vietnam in the Army JAG, JAG lawyer.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And so I said: I think I got it. And a couple of -- shortly thereafter I got orders to go in the summer of 1968.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And what was it that -- I mean, you did volunteer?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I thought it was my job to go. I mean the -- I remember a friend of mine in World War II. I was a young guy and I was going with his daughter. And he volunteered to go into the Army and be recalled to active duty. He was some kind of reservist. And he was an older guy. He was a banker and everything. And I said: Carl, why did you do this? He said: The world is playing a game, and I don't like the game, but I want to be in on it. Well, I thought it would be a terrible thing if I had spent my life in the Army as I was now up to 25 years and not have really been doing something significant and so I said: I want that job in Vietnam. I don't like what we're doing in Vietnam particulary. I don't like why we're there. But that's not my -- I didn't make that decision.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And if I want to be -- if I'm so anti, then I have to change my approach about what I'm doing in life. And I felt that I had a responsibility and I wanted to do it. But if I was going to do it, I didn't want to continue to be doing something else. And I had a good job.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I had a good job at Fort Riley. I was well liked and everything was going well and people were taking nice care of me and blah, blah, blah, blah. And I wanted to go and I think that my wife understood.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Whether my kids did or not, but they do.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Now at the time you did that, did you have any personal feelings about the war because obviously the Vietnam war was one that a lot of people had different perspectives on? Or, again, were you kind of looking at it as your job?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I looked at it as my job. I wasn't trying to end the war. There was no way that I was going to end it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But I wanted to do it my way. I wanted to be there and I did and I went over; and, fortunately, it worked out well for me. I was very fortunate to have the kind job I did. I enjoyed doing it. I thought I made -- I thought I made, how do you want to say it, I did something -- I did some worthwhile things. Sometimes you only -- only thing you do is put out fires.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I had been there -- give you a quick story. I had been there about a week when I made -- and one of the things that judges or the Judge Advocate always has to do is being concerned about the stockade. The stockade in Vietnam was called the Long Binh Jail. Now you can figure out that means LBJ. Well, I made my tour. My office was probably 500 yards away from LBJ. I made my tour and I made the tour and I said: This is awful. It was built for 250 people. And they have 700 in here. The guards aren't running it. The prisoners are. They're deciding who sleeps in what bed. So I went back to talk to Provost Marshal General or Provost Marshal, who was a friend of mine, Karl Gustafson. And he wasn't very interested. He had just been named Provost Marshal General and was about to leave for Washington and he didn't sound very interested. So I went to see the General. And I said: We got to do something about this. I said: This can't go on. At least we got to get people out of there.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We got to separate them out. He said: How are you going to do it? I said: Well, first of all, some of them have long terms. And they shouldn't be in that jail. They should send them to Japan for jail or Okinawa or Hawaii or back to the States. They aren't being moved as they should be. I said: We can do that. I said -- then I got a smart idea. I was a smart alec. I said: General, soldiers ought to be fighting. They shouldn't be in jail. Well, that struck a note with him. I said: These people got sent there for pretty much minor crimes in many cases, marijuana, drugs, insubordination. There weren't any people who were murderers and so forth, although there were some.
