And I said: Units don't want them back. They sent them there, and they want them to stay for their whole time they're supposed to be put in jail. If they got a six months' jail sentence, they want them there for six months.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: He said: What can you do about it? I said: We'll make them take them back; or we'll put them on parole or probation or just change their sentence because I said: We have the authority to do it. Good. Good, Judge. That's what I want to do. So we went back, and we set up a program in the office to do it. And we were going to start it on day one. And I came out of my office that morning because I was flying up to some other unit I wanted to see. I noticed this fire, all this black smoke. I was a day late. The prisoners burned down the stockade. And they killed two or three people. And so we got in, of course, we kept them. Some escaped. Few escaped, not many. And they were inside. And it was outside. There was a big fence all around the whole place. You couldn't get out. So the General says: What are you going to do? I said: Well, we can go in and get them. No, he says. It's not worth the life or damage to any M P to send them in there and get those guys, shoot them or something. So I said: Okay. Let's see, he said: So give them food. Throw food over the fence, run some water in there. Well, they did for several days. Well, that got to be old. I went back and said: I've got a new idea. So we went down, and we had all the names. We knew who was in there --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- because we had their list. So my Chief of Military Justice, George Russell, stood at the gate; and he called them out one by one by name. As the guy came up, he said: Leave. And they all left. They didn't want to stay there. It was hot in that sun. And they were only getting food thrown over and it was --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- they were being kept in by the leadership. So we got them all out and then we went to trial on a bunch that we knew were the ring leaders and so on, so that ended that. Unfortunately, then we built a new stockade with a lot of different approaches to it. That was my most interesting. Little side light to that if I may tell --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- because it's funny. We had a civilian contractor who stole a cherry picker and a power shovel and something else, big equipment and got them put on a ship to the Philippines. He sold them. Well, we caught him. We knew who did it. So we decided, well, what are we going to do about him because this is a time when we didn't know whether we could try civilians in Military Court. So I said: Go down and get his passport. But we were a day late again. He was on his way to Thailand. So I called my JA friend in Thailand and I said go get this guy off of there. Well, they said: We don't think that the Thais would like that. I don't care if the Thais like it. He got out and started to fly to Hong Kong. Well, there was a hurricane, typhoon. And he was diverted to Japan. So I called Japan. I said: I think he's carrying a weapon. The Japanese said: Okay. Pick him up and fly him back. Well, they flew him back and we picked him up. Then what do we do with him? So I said: Well, we've got one stockade. We'll put him in the stockade. Do you know what a Conex container is?

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Okay. I said: Take one of those Conex containers. Cut a door in it. Cut a window in it. Put him in there. So we put him in there. We put him in the day before they burned up the stockade. So I thought, oh, God. We've got a roasted civilian. Well, he made it through all right. We got him out of there. This is a long story. Finally we flew him to the United States, and he was tried by Federal District Court and was convicted and so forth. Part of the problems -- you talk about the problems. I mean, that was peanuts to the problems I was concerned with. But it's the kind of thing or that's a funny little sidelights to life.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The takeover of the stockade, the LBJ stockade, was that an unusual circumstance; or was that something --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: It was right after Attica. And I thought, oh, we're going to get -- the Army is going to get the worse possible publicity. We never got a word. I had them put out a press release. I went to the PR guys to put out a press release that two were killed. Nobody ever paid any attention to it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Do you think it was inspired by Attica? Do you think it was something that they had heard about? What caused it?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Race. It was a racial thing. I'm sorry. But it's the truth.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, having gone through World War II and Korea and Vietnam, were -- were the racial issues new in Vietnam; or was there dynamic that had existed all along; or was there something that changed between Vietnam --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Well, you got to remember that Truman changed the whole thing in the midst of the Korean war. So we didn't have long to kind of live with this thing before we got into Vietnam. And I'm sure there was a lot of racial implications to who was confined and how many were confined. I mean, I'm a big boy. I know that life is like that. I think it was wrong. I know all the wrong questions. It's a terrible thing that we do these things, but it was -- it was what was a fact. And I know that there were gangs that were saying, okay, this guy sleep in this bed. Okay. That's not really the way you run a stockade.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Let me ask. We've got few more minutes because we have some time constraints.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: But I'm curious within the JAG corps on the racial issues, were there very many minority attorneys being able to represent the minority soldiers that were charged with offenses; and how was the ratio of minority participation in the JAG corps related to the minority participation in the soldiers at large from what you saw?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: There were almost none. I went on a recruiting trip in 1950 something or other and went to all the big ten schools area. And somebody asked me then, in the other report that you have, had we tried to recruit women or minorities. I said: Absolutely not. We didn't pay attention to them. This was the 1950s.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: When I became the Commandant of the Judge Advocate General School, which was right after I left Vietnam or a year after I left Vietnam, the first thing I called the Pentagon and said: I want a Black teacher and a woman to come out and I want two on my staff who will teach on the platform.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And by that time we were beginning to recruit people. We didn't recruit them much. There weren't many of them. I don't -- I'm having trouble. And I don't remember anyone. There may have been one or two in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But I don't remember. I had -- my best officer was a Chinese, who became a Judge Advocate General of the Army who came here when he was 16 from China --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- with his family. And so the opportunity for saying there is no racism.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Nright.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: At least in that part of the world could be easily refuted.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We have -- we have a Brigadier General about to be a Major General in JAG corps now who is a woman.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I mean, it's all changed.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: But in the time of the Vietnam and that LBJ incident --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: There wasn't.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- it really wasn't a representation?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No. There wasn't. I don't remember -- come to think of it, I don't remember any. I don't remember any and I was assigning everybody, not assigning, but I mean, I was seeing where people went. And we had a lot of them. First thing I did when I got to Vietnam, I said: I need 20 more lawyers.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I'll tell you one more thing before I forget it, because you'll like this. The next thing I did was, I said: We've got to have some court reporters here. I had two in my office, two women, American, court reporters in my office. And we were trying to cover Vietnam. Well, this is silly.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I mean I was sending them to the big cases and that's the only one. And then we had some other people around who were able to really use stenographers. So I said: We can't go on this way. We've got dozens of cases. We've got to send a transcribed case for review. I did stop transcribing not guilties. We used to send them. I stopped doing that. I just wrote the --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- Pentagon we weren't going to do that anymore. I didn't hear any reply so I guess it was all right. So then we worked it out this way. I had a Warrant Officer Clay Butler. He was Black as a matter of fact. He was not a lawyer. And I said: Clay, we got to do something about this. So he would go over to where they brought in all the new -- the depot where they brought in people from the United States. He would get the records and see somebody who was a college graduate, who could type. And he would say to this guy, they would be 11 Bravo. 11 Bravo is the key number for an infantryman. Well, these guys all came in. They had all been drafted, still the draft was on and they had all been drafted and they were 11 Bravos. If you say to somebody: Would you like to be a court reporter? And he says: Or would you like to go on up to the front to 11 Bravo? I'll be a court reporter.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right; right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: So we bring these guys back and bring them to the office. We take them ten or 12 at a time. And we teach them the Gray Audiograph. You don't even know what a Gray Audiograph is? Well, we had plenty of them. And this is the thing where the guy sits in the courtroom with the mask. And he repeats everything he hears in the courtroom and then he takes it back and from that transcription, he types up the record of trial. And so we -- we were making our own court reporters because it's the only way we could do it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And it worked out fine. Now you don't get what you get. But, as you know, you miss something on points. I bet once you've missed some words said in court. THE COURT REPORTER: Maybe more than one. (Laughter)

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But at any rate, this was my experience with court reporting in Vietnam. The very first thing I got there I said: I want 20 more Captains.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Because I need people to try cases and I need court reporters. Well, I made my own court reporters. I couldn't make my Captains.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And finally, when you're in Vietnam, everything was prescribed. You could have some of this and so many of that and so many of the other. To get 20 new lawyer JAGs, I had to -- and we changed the law. We always changed the law in the middle of the war. We changed it in the middle of Korea. And we changed it in the middle of Vietnam to put it much different way of running a court martial. And I went to the Command I said: We got to have them. They said: We don't have any spaces. I said: You have to take them. They took them from somebody else. I don't know who they took them from but they gave me 20 additional spaces for Captains so we could try to cases.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Let me ask one more area of questions and then I'd like to see if my son has any prospectus from the younger side and see if you have any questions. Then I ask one more question and I think we're hitting our time limit. Actually, probably two more questions. One question I have is you mentioned the fact that in Vietnam and LBJ stockade, there were a number of people there for drug offenses between the -- what you saw in World War II and Korea and in Vietnam, was there a change in drug use in the military? And did you see that as having any major impact on how the wars were conducted or on the types of issues the JAG Corps had to deal with?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Let me say this about drugs. When I returned from Vietnam, I made a number of newspaper interviews around places because I would go give a speech and then the press would get involved. And I said that I thought that the use of drugs began in October of 19 -- that would be '68. Yeah. This was my personal view. And I thought, it was my own personal opinion, was that it was caused, that the Chinese pushed it. I thought this was their contribution to the Vietnam war. It started to -- too much on a -- at one time. And I got there there wasn't much use of it. There was use of marijuana. But don't misunderstand what I'm going to say next. In Vietnam, the Vietnam period, we drafted -- how am I going to say this without sounding totally something or other -- we drafted people -- we didn't draft people who would have been drafted in World War II and who might not have been drafted in Korea. We let them all go to college and let them get deferments and so forth and so on.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: So the draft from Vietnam was predominately at a less educated, less income, lower social economic group as opposed to Korea and World War II --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: What you're saying is correct.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: -- which may have had a more full spectrum of America?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I think these people came from a part of America where the use of drugs was not frowned upon as much as it -- of course, now apparently in America, everybody uses drugs. I don't know. I went through a period of life that I couldn't believe what I was living through; but anyway, I think that that was part of it. And I think -- and the drug use wasn't bad. It wasn't massive.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Even in Vietnam. But the people, if you wanted to get rid of somebody out of the unit who was a no good, a slacker, had some other problems, well, you found him guilty of -- you would -- you could find him -- it wasn't a question he didn't do it.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And then you send him to LBJ and you got rid of him.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Now I don't think a lot of people did that. Don't misunderstand me. Lot of people probably just as many senior sergeants --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- smoking marijuana as these lower ranking people. But it seemed to me there was a different problem than the people in -- I don't know if there's any use particularly, or at least we didn't discuss it, in World War II and very little -- I know that it was going on in Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: You mentioned that Chinese you thought had a big role in that?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: And the Chinese were involved in both Korea and Vietnam. Do you think they were intentionally --

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But they were not down inside our villages. Don't forget, the Chinese were north --

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: -- of the line. In Vietnam there wasn't any north of the line.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: We never knew -- never knew if the little women who were the maids or the waitresses, whether they were carrying some kind of weapon underneath or carrying a bomb or whatever. I never had any problem as far as I was concerned, but I have pictures in my own scrap books of our post office which was bombed, I mean, down the hall from my office.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. By a suicide bomber?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: No, just by -- but that's how close they got in. If you look at Vietnam, we were 50 miles out of Saigon. And the border of Vietnam or South Vietnam or North Vietnam was way to the north of that, but down in this area, down below us, down in the delta, everywhere, there were people in the pajamas, black pajamas.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Sure. So I guess the overall stress level never went away because you never knew whether you were 3 feet or 30 miles from an enemy?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: That's right. That's right. You may have been safer up in a unit up in a division than you were down in Saigon.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Because they all look alike.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Because they're all Vietnamese.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. Now we're getting close to I think a time limit they've set us for these interviews. I'd just like to ask you as a final question knowing that this transcript is going to be submitted for Library of Congress records, you know, are there anything or anythings that you would like to make sure are documented for history with respect to your military career?

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Oh, I don't have much of a career. I loved every minute that I was serving. I did have some bosses I didn't like. But I don't regret one minute of my military career. I was fortunate. God looked after me some ways. I had a family that supported me in everything I did, both my parents, my wife and my children. I did very well. I would have liked to do more, obviously. But I have no, no regrets at all. I still am a soldier. When I call on the phone, I say, this is Colonel Douglass. And I'm proud to do it. And I was awarded all of -- more metals and stuff than I probably deserve. And I've got great friends. After the -- after I left the corps, after I left the Army, I formed -- I went to Korea, as a matter of fact, with a group of people who had been in Korea during the war. And when we came back, we said: You know that was great trip. It was fun. All of us going together, all of us former lawyers. Why don't we do this more often? So a friend of mine and I started something call RAJA, R-A-J-A, Regular Army Judge Advocates. And for 20 years -- well, now let's see, 22 years, maybe more than that, 24 years, something like that. They've been meeting once a year. And all retired officers, these are career officers and their families, meet once a year some place. Last year they were in Fort Worth. For 14 years I was the president of that organization. We never had elections. That's why. And another fellow and I ran it for a number of years. And I'm very close to all those people. I mean, I -- these are my buddies. These are my friends. These are the people that I served with, not just in Korea, but in Germany, in Heidelberg, in Panama and wherever. They are my close friends in life to this day. Of course, unfortunately, in my case because I'm 90, mine are dying. And I -- that's why I hate to pick up one of my emails when I see it's coming from a certain group from RAJA people because I know somebody else is gone. I've just -- it was a great career. And I don't regret it one minute. And I don't find anything I did that I wish I hadn't done. I find some things I wish I had done and didn't do.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: But as far as the rest is concerned, I have no misgivings.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, I just want to tell you on behalf of myself and my son, I think we all, and the court reporter, everybody here, I think, thanks you for all the service that you had. And I think really if you look at just the career, you've been able to talk about over the last hour and 40 minutes, it's extensive, expansive and inspiring in a lot of ways. I mean, there are so many people who don't take initiative to do the right thing. The fact that you came back and didn't like the 52-20 and felt the need to push on, the fact that you volunteered for Vietnam, you know, that you took some initiative in trying to make sure that you were integrating the JAG Corps and bringing women and seeing others representative, I think is inspiring. And, you know, I'm excited that this has been been recorded. Because I think this is something people need to know about. I think what you did has left and will leave a lasting impact on the country and the military.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: I think you underestimate yourself if you think you haven't done that. You know, as a personal matter, you know, based on the other information you had, you've obviously made a huge impact on the world with your family. So I think few people leave those kind of wakes in the world. And I think you ought to be very proud of that.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I remember the first female lawyer, she worked for me. The first one I ever met was Mary Attaya. I was in Japan and I was doing some work in Tokyo. The office was in Tokyo. And she was there. And she was a WAC. She wasn't a JAG because we didn't have anyplace in the JAG for women. But she was a WAC lawyer. So we brought her in and put her to work. But later I got to know Mary very well and then I met another one. I can't remember her name -- Mary -- it's awful. Anyway, and then finally now they're all over, you know.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: And I have a great friend who was Associate Dean at West Virginia who was now -- who was the first JAG Black Major General.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Well, wonderful.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: He's been out. He's been retired for 15 years at least.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: I tell you. We really thank you for your service. And thank you for participating in this program.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: I wanted to do this.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: As I said: I'm trying to write the story what I did after I left the Army. And looking forward to.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: That would be great to do that.

sp.speaker: John J. Douglass
sp.p: Because I ran the National College of District Attorneys for 20 years and had some real experiences there. And I was reading yesterday the new Criminal Justice Magazine that comes out of ABA. And I thought, we were talking these same things 25 years ago that they're raising now.

sp.speaker: Robert McAughan
sp.p: Right. Great. We'll go ahead and take a break. (End of interview)
